title: Words, Statements, and Arguments
summary: Reading and vocabulary on ambiguity, statements, arguments, premises, conclusions, and argument quality.

blocks.html:
As Isocrates writes, the mark of humanityÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s genius is discourse, the ability to reason with one another about what is good, true, and beautiful. Our arts, from poetry and painting, to architecture and economics, to engineering and education, are built on the capacity to discuss and reason together and persuade each other to believe truly, act well, improve ourselves and the world, and appreciate whatever is valuable. In this course, we will learn a few skills to improve our faculties of discourse.

Logic is, broadly, the study of methods for evaluating how well statements support (or give evidence for) a conclusion. That is, logic helps us to see why we should or should not believe something. If you propose a hypothesis, the data should fit your hypothesis at least as well as rival hypotheses. If you approach your boss to ask for a raise, you had better have some evidence that your work is worth the extra payment. If you are discussing politics, you should be willing to provide reasons for why a certain policy would be good to adopt, and likewise listen and carefully consider the reasons given by your discussion partner who may disagree with you. If you are diagnosing an illness (whether you are a doctor or just looking up your symptoms on WebMD), it is important to factor in not only your symptoms, but other factors which affect the likelihood of you having some medical problem. If a friend is considering hastily breaking up with their partner, you might want to help them reconsider. An understanding of logic will help to navigate much of the world, from large issues like religion and politics to the mundane ones.

In this introduction, weÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ll be looking briefly at the way language shapes thinking and argumentation (and vice versa) before moving onto some features of arguments. The rest of the course will be devoted to exploring what makes arguments to be good arguments.

If youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ve ever walked into a craftsmanÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s toolshed, an automobile shop, or a Ã¢â‚¬Å“makerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s space,Ã¢â‚¬Â youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ve seen walls and cabinets full of tools. And if youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re as inexperienced in craftsmanship as I am, youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ll go dizzy with just how many different tools there are. They all must have some purpose, but aside from a few universal tools, like hammers, I couldnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t tell you what they are for. And even familiar tools might have cousins that I could recognize as a Ã¢â‚¬Å“hammerÃ¢â‚¬Â but not be able to give their precise purpose. A mallet is a kind of hammer, but you wouldnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t want to try to use it on a nail.

Words are like tools in two major ways. First, single words, like single tools, might be used for many purposes. A flathead (Ã¢â‚¬â€œ) screwdriver, for instance, can turn flathead screws, but it can also turn screws meant to take a Philips head (+) screwdriver. It can also pry open paint cans or be used as a small chisel. Likewise, one word or phrase might have a number of uses. I donÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t mean that the word Ã¢â‚¬Å“bearÃ¢â‚¬Â can mean both Ã¢â‚¬Å“the Chicago baseball teamÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s large, furry, ursine mascotÃ¢â‚¬Â as well as Ã¢â‚¬Å“to carry something heavy.Ã¢â‚¬Â I mean that we might say that one person Ã¢â‚¬Å“bears a burdenÃ¢â‚¬Â when they are moving heavy boxes a long distance, and another person Ã¢â‚¬Å“bears a burdenÃ¢â‚¬Â when they are emotionally distraught by something that happened in their past. Notice that these arenÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t entirely separate meanings Ã¢â‚¬â€œ carrying something physically weighty is very much like carrying something emotionally weighty. These are two different senses, ways of using, the same word Ã¢â‚¬Å“bearÃ¢â‚¬Â (or the phrase Ã¢â‚¬Å“bears a burdenÃ¢â‚¬Â).

The second way words are like tools is that some words are better for some jobs than others. While you can use a flathead screwdriver for a Philips screw, you canÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t use a Philips screwdriver for a flathead screw. You can use a flathead screwdriver like a chisel, but often it would be much better to use a real chisel. Likewise, even if words can be used in many ways, they canÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t be used in unlimited ways. If I told you Ã¢â‚¬Å“Jim bore his burdenÃ¢â‚¬Â to refer to Jim dropping the crates he was carrying, I would not be communicating effectively to you Ã¢â‚¬â€œ no one takes Ã¢â‚¬Å“bearÃ¢â‚¬Â to be used to talk about someone dropping something. The limitations on wordsÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ uses is what makes words meaningful. This is also why it is often better not to use a thesaurus when writing essays. Words that have very similar meanings can have precise uses that donÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t fit the purpose. For example, if you look up Ã¢â‚¬Å“exaggeratedÃ¢â‚¬Â in the thesaurus, one of the synonyms will be Ã¢â‚¬Å“fabricated.Ã¢â‚¬Â ThereÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s a sense in which exaggerations are fabricated Ã¢â‚¬â€œ the fish wasnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t really two feet long, it was more like ten inches. The extra inches are made up, fabricated. But fabricated is usually used to mean something entirely made up, whereas one exaggerates when the story is only partially made up. Someone bragging about the fish they caught might really have caught a fish, and the fish really was large Ã¢â‚¬â€œ just not quite as large as they exaggeratedly claimed.

When thinking, discussing, and reasoning, be attentive to the different uses of words. This is such an important skill to practice in your daily life. Often, people misunderstand each other because each are using the same words in different ways. You may find that the words youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re using are ambiguous; that is, you could be very unclear to your conversation partner which precise purpose youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re using the words for. When you or your conversation partner is using a word ambiguously, one or both of you needs to draw a distinction. To draw a distinction is to explicitly state, and differentiate, multiple senses of an ambiguous term. This is one of the main skills which I hope to teach you throughout the semester. (IÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ve heard it said that philosophy is the art of drawing distinctions.) When I explained the difference between Ã¢â‚¬Å“bears a burdenÃ¢â‚¬Â as an emotional bearing and a physical bearing, I drew a distinction between the two uses of the term/phrase.

HereÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s an example of when drawing distinctions is important for more controversial topics. I used to volunteer for an organization in Boston which seeks to bring different Christian churches of all denominations together for dialogue and service. After 1,000 years of schism between Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Christians, and 500 years of the separation between Roman Catholic and Protestant Christians, the different major Christian bodies might be speaking the same natural language (English, say), but be speaking entirely different theological languages. The ability to draw distinctions and point out ambiguities is vital. An Evangelical Protestant might ask a Roman Catholic, for instance, Ã¢â‚¬Å“Have you been saved?Ã¢â‚¬Â This is probably the most important question to most Evangelicals. However, notice that the use of this word is past tensed; Ã¢â‚¬Å“being savedÃ¢â‚¬Â is used to indicate a single event that would happen in oneÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s life. Indeed, Ã¢â‚¬Å“salvation,Ã¢â‚¬Â as they use the term, is a single event in oneÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s past: an acknowledgement of oneÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s dependence on JesusÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ sacrifice and commitment to follow JesusÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ teachings and example, which is the moment when JesusÃ¢â‚¬â„¢ sacrifice applies to that person, forgiving their sins. To a Catholic (or Eastern Orthodox, or other Protestant), the question sounds like a very strange use of the word Ã¢â‚¬Å“salvation.Ã¢â‚¬Â The question (Ã¢â‚¬Å“Have you been saved?Ã¢â‚¬Â) is relatively unimportant to them not because salvation is unimportant, but because the very question sounds like someone who is not quite fluent in their language (though itÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s the most perfectly natural question in the Evangelical language). This is because, as Catholics use the term, Ã¢â‚¬Å“salvationÃ¢â‚¬Â applies to the future, to the eventual full union between that person and God through the sacrifice of Jesus, which sacrifice transforms that person to be more like Jesus throughout their life. Perhaps the question Ã¢â‚¬Å“Have you been saved?Ã¢â‚¬Â is closest, for the Catholic, to the question Ã¢â‚¬Å“Have you been baptized?Ã¢â‚¬Â. Both questions ask about the beginning of the Christian life, when sin is first forgiven and the Christian begins his or her journey toward God. However, like Ã¢â‚¬Å“exaggeratedÃ¢â‚¬Â and Ã¢â‚¬Å“fabricated,Ã¢â‚¬Â the Protestant Ã¢â‚¬Å“savedÃ¢â‚¬Â doesnÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t mean the same thing as the Catholic Ã¢â‚¬Å“baptism,Ã¢â‚¬Â but they do bear important similarities. Fruitful conversation between Christian groups (and any other group, religious or otherwise) requires mutual understanding, which can only be had when each side learns to use important words as the other side does.

If youÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re thinking that only religious language is this complicated, allow me to list ambiguous words which often come up in secular public discourse: rights, opinion, man, woman, gender, fact, reasonable, good, purpose, nature, technology, person, human, immigration, race, racism, justice, force, equalityÃ¢â‚¬Â¦the list goes on. One reason for our increasing political polarization is that people do not use these words to mean the same things Ã¢â‚¬â€œ but donÃ¢â‚¬â„¢t realize that theyÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re speaking different conceptual languages.

Moving from the very general to our particular interests in logic, the kinds of collections of words weÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re concerned with are arguments, which are composed of statements. LetÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s draw a distinction between statements and sentences. A sentence is any grammatically correct piece of speech or writing with a subject and predicate. A statement is a declarative (or descriptive) sentence that is either true or false. The following are statements:

Not all dogs are collies.

Jones spent 3 hours at the Salvation Army.

The judgeÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s sentence fit the crime.

YouÃ¢â‚¬â„¢re wrong about her.

The following are not statements:

Do you own a collie?

Go to the Salvation Army.

Incredible!

Questions, commands, and exclamations are neither true nor false, and so those sentences are not statements.

An argument is a set of statements where some of the statements are intended to support another. The conclusion is the statement to be supported, while the premises are the statements which are meant to support the conclusion. Consider the following very simple argument:

ItÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s raining. Therefore, you should bring an umbrella.
